response.executive_summary: Assessment asm-001 examined Husky AI on the basis of two supplied documents, security-notes.md (src-001) and system-overview.md (src-002); both were reviewed and ingested, and their evidence was available to every stage of the analysis. The assessment produced four approved findings: one of high severity, fnd-005, concerning the execution of attacker code inside the production web server when a tampered serialized model is loaded; and three of medium severity, fnd-001 (an unverified model artifact written into the production model blob and served), fnd-006 (injected code or configuration in the source storage packaged and delivered into production), and fnd-007 (Bastion access logs altered or deleted by an actor holding the production access those logs record). Each of the four records a requirement as partially satisfied for its threat, and each carries the recommendation to establish whether the requirement is met and to record the control that meets it. Seven controls were confirmed on the evidence: Bastion SSH access logging, access control on the Jupyter Notebook environment and its confinement to the experimental VPC (recorded twice, as ctl-005 and ctl-011, against different threats), transport encryption on the public API and the Azure Cognitive Services image collection path (ctl-006 and ctl-009), the holding of uploaded images in memory only in the Redis cache, and per-environment access control on the source code and configuration storage. No documentation gaps were approved. Nineteen questions remain open: three of high priority, covering access control on the API key, authorized keys and Bastion log stores; whether end users are authenticated when submitting images to the public classification API; and whether the packaged model artifact is integrity-verified between being written in the experimental environment and being loaded in production. Fifteen further questions are of medium priority and one of low priority. Several matters therefore could not be determined from the material supplied, and the three limitations recorded below state the assumptions on which fnd-005, fnd-006 and fnd-007 rest.
response.system_overview: Husky AI, as described by the approved system context, is a public image classification service built around a trained convolutional neural network, with a production serving path and a separate experimental environment in which images are gathered and the model is produced. Fifteen components were approved. On the production side these are the API Gateway (cmp-001), a Simple Python Web Server (cmp-002), a Bastion Server (cmp-003), an Azure Cache for Redis instance (cmp-013), and the Machine Learning Model blob (cmp-010). On the experimental and supply side they are the Gather Images Application (cmp-004), a Jupyter Notebook environment (cmp-005), a Deployment Service (cmp-006), and the Training and Validation Images blob (cmp-007). Supporting stores are the API Key storage (cmp-008), the Source Code and Configuration storage (cmp-009), the Authorized Keys storage (cmp-011) and the Bastion Logs storage (cmp-012). Two external dependencies complete the set: Azure Cognitive Services (cmp-014) and third-party image tools (cmp-015). Four actor groups interact with the system: end users (act-001), data engineers (act-002), Azure platform engineers (act-003), and the external services themselves, Azure Cognitive Services and the third-party tools (act-004). Eight assets were approved: the trained convolutional neural network model (ast-001), the training and validation images (ast-002), the API keys for external image services (ast-003), the source code and configuration (ast-004), the SSH authorized keys (ast-005), the Bastion SSH access and activity logs (ast-006), user-uploaded images awaiting classification (ast-007), and the availability of the public classification service (ast-008). Seventeen data flows connect these parts. Images arrive at the Gather Images application from Azure Cognitive Services (df-001) and from third-party tools (df-002), with the application reading API keys (df-003) and writing the collected images to the training blob (df-004). The Jupyter environment reads the training and validation images (df-005) and writes the serialized model to the model storage blob (df-006). The deployment service reads the trained model for packaging (df-007) and the source code and configuration (df-008), and delivers releases into production through the Bastion (df-009). The Bastion reads authorized keys for SSH authentication (df-010), writes SSH access and session logs (df-011), and provides administrative access to the API Gateway (df-012), to the Python web server (df-013) and to the model blob (df-014). In the serving path, the API Gateway forwards classification requests to the web server (df-015), the web server holds uploaded images in the Redis cache (df-016), and the web server loads the trained model from the model blob (df-017). Three trust boundaries were approved: public internet to production (tb-001), public internet to experimental (tb-002), and production to experimental (tb-003). The confirmed controls sit along these boundaries in specific places: the public API is documented as HTTPS-only and the Azure Cognitive Services collection path as using TLS with server certificate validation, the Jupyter Notebook environment is documented as authenticated and not exposed outside the experimental VPC, all SSH access attempts through the Bastion are logged to the Bastion Logs storage, uploaded images are documented as held in memory in the Redis cache rather than written to disk, and access control on the Azure Blob storage accounts, including the source and configuration storage, is documented as granted per environment. The documentation does not extend the transport statements to the internal production flows, does not make an equivalent TLS statement for the third-party image tools, and does not distinguish read from write in the per-environment blob access control.
response.risk_summary: The four approved findings concentrate almost entirely on one theme: the integrity of what moves from the lower-trust experimental environment into production, and the difficulty of detecting a change once it has moved. Three of the four findings sit on that path. fnd-001, at medium severity, describes a substituted or altered model artifact written into the production model blob and served without verification, with the consequence that the classification behaviour of the public service is controlled by the actor and no documented artifact verification would reveal the substitution. fnd-005, the single high-severity finding, extends the same write into code execution inside the production web server when the tampered serialized model is loaded, giving the actor the server's access to the model artifact, to user-uploaded images held in the cache, and the ability to stop or corrupt the serving path. fnd-006, at medium severity, reaches the same destination by a different route: injected code or configuration in the source storage, packaged and delivered into production, changing how uploaded images are handled, how the model is loaded, or whether the service functions at all. Two of these three, fnd-005 and fnd-006, record the same requirement, req-CICD-001, as partially satisfied for their respective threats; fnd-001 records req-ADMIN-001 as partially satisfied. The fourth finding, fnd-007 at medium severity, concerns the record rather than the act: Bastion access logs altered or deleted by an actor holding the production access those logs record, with the loss of the ability to attribute or reconstruct administrative actions in production, including tampering with the model artifact, which the impact statement notes would otherwise be visible only through this record. It records req-LOG-002 as partially satisfied. Taken together, the set describes a system whose production serving behaviour is derived from artifacts produced elsewhere, where the assessment found no documented verification step at the point of use, and where the one confirmed logging control, Bastion SSH access logging, is itself the subject of an integrity finding. Two confirmed controls bound the picture rather than closing it: uploaded images are documented as held in memory only in the Redis cache, which limits what an actor with execution inside the production web server could recover to images resident at that time, and access control on the source and configuration storage is documented as granted per environment, though the same passage does not distinguish read from write nor restrict which experimental principals may modify content that will be packaged into production. The recommendation attached to every one of the four findings is the same in form: establish whether the requirement is met for the threat, and record the control that meets it. Each finding also carries its own recorded limitation on the reasoning behind it. For fnd-001, the step between a completed write and a changed decision function is missing from the preconditions, because the cited passages do not say when the web server reads the artifact. For fnd-005, only the first entry branch, a write to the model blob along a documented write path, is supported; the alternative branch of modifying the release while it is packaged and delivered through the Bastion is not established by the cited passages. For fnd-006, the entry condition of write access to the source storage for experimental principals is presented as documented but is not carried by the cited passage, which names no principals and does not distinguish read from write. For fnd-007, the acting principal's modify or delete permission on the Bastion Logs storage appears in neither the preconditions nor the cited passages. These recorded limitations qualify the strength of the reasoning, not the reviewer-assigned severities, which stand as assigned. What the findings do not settle, the open questions do not settle either. It could not be determined whether the packaged model artifact is integrity-verified between being written in the experimental environment and being loaded by the production web server, how access is controlled to the API key, authorized keys and Bastion log stores, whether end users are authenticated at the public classification endpoint, whether internal production flows are authenticated and encrypted in transit, whether data is encrypted at rest in the blob accounts and the cache, how long uploaded images are retained, what protects the Redis instance, whether the third-party image collection path uses TLS with certificate validation, from which networks the Bastion is reachable, what validation is applied to uploaded image content, whether the authorization posture is deny-by-default, what logging and log protection exist beyond Bastion SSH logging, whether uploaded images can contain sensitive data, how the deployment service and notebook environment authenticate to the model storage account, what access and immutability configuration applies to the Bastion Logs storage, what the web server's dependencies are, what rate, size or concurrency limits apply to the classification endpoint, how the web server and production model blob are placed and reachable on the network, and how the external-service API keys are provisioned, rotated and scoped. Several of these bear directly on the findings above: an answer to the artifact-verification question in particular would change how fnd-001 and fnd-005 should be read. No documentation gaps were approved, so the unresolved matters are carried by these open questions rather than by gap records.

limitations.text: Finding fnd-005 rests on a stated assumption rather than on an explicit statement in the documentation. The assessment took the public-key authentication described for movement between production and experimental, in evd-007 and evd-009, to be the mechanism by which the deployment service authenticates through the Bastion. The documentation does not say so explicitly. If the deployment service authenticates by some other mechanism, the reasoning behind this high-severity finding would need to be revisited, and a reviewer should treat that link in the chain as assumed rather than established.

Finding fnd-006 rests on a stated assumption rather than on an explicit statement in the documentation. The assessment took the public-key authentication described for movement between production and experimental, in evd-007 and evd-009, to be the mechanism by which the deployment service authenticates to the Bastion, on the basis that evd-012 describes the delivery over that same path. This is an inference the assessment recorded as an assumption, not a documented fact, and the finding should be read with that qualification in place.

Finding fnd-007 rests on a stated assumption rather than on an explicit statement in the documentation. The assessment assumed that the activity logs named in the store inventory, evd-011, are SSH session records rather than per-object records of writes to the model blob. The documentation does not state which they are. If those logs are in fact per-object write records, or cover a different scope again, the impact described for this finding on the ability to attribute or reconstruct administrative actions would need to be reassessed.
